note: Hand-curated. radius km; a = semi-major axis (AU around the Sun, km around a planet); period in years (heliocentric) or days (moons). el = osculating elements for bodies placed from a Kepler orbit: a AU, e, i, node, peri (argument), M0 at epoch (JD), period yr; good to about a degree. Planets use JPL elements in js/astro.js. look = [surface model, three colours, strength]: 0 cratered rock, 1 banded gas, 2 cracked ice, 3 haze, 4 star, 5 Earth. rings = inner and outer radius, km.

bodies.name: Sun
bodies.note: A G2 dwarf holding 99.86% of the Solar System's mass. Light from its surface reaches Earth in about 8 min 19 s; the energy made in its core takes on the order of a hundred thousand years to work its way out.

bodies.name: Mercury
bodies.note: Locked in a 3:2 spin–orbit resonance, so one solar day lasts two Mercury years. BepiColombo, a European–Japanese mission, is due to enter orbit on 21 November 2026.

bodies.name: Venus
bodies.note: Nearly Earth's twin in size, with a 92-bar carbon dioxide atmosphere and a surface hot enough to melt lead. It rotates backwards, once every 243 days.

bodies.name: Earth
bodies.note: The only place known to host life. Every light-time on this site is measured from here. The coastlines and the 4,584 city lights are real, and the line between day and night is where it is right now.

bodies.name: Mars
bodies.note: A cold desert with dry river valleys, polar caps and ice below the surface. Its distance from Earth swings between about 3 and 22 light-minutes, which is why rovers cannot be driven live.

bodies.name: Jupiter
bodies.note: More than twice as massive as all the other planets together. The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been watched for at least 190 years. The four large moons shown around it are where they really are right now.

bodies.name: Saturn
bodies.note: Its rings span 280,000 km yet are typically tens of metres thick. The tilt you see here is the real one for today. Saturn is less dense than water.

bodies.name: Uranus
bodies.note: Tipped 98° onto its side, so each pole gets 42 years of sunlight and then 42 of darkness. Visited once, by Voyager 2 in January 1986.

bodies.name: Neptune
bodies.note: Found in 1846 at the position predicted from its pull on Uranus. Its winds are the fastest measured on any planet, about 2,000 km/h.

bodies.name: Moon
bodies.note: Formed from the debris of a giant impact about 4.5 billion years ago and receding from Earth at 3.8 cm a year. Laser pulses bounced off reflectors left by Apollo and Lunokhod measure the distance to millimetres. Its position and phase here are today's.

bodies.name: Phobos
bodies.note: Orbits Mars faster than Mars rotates, so it rises in the west. Tides are drawing it inward; within about 50 million years it will break up or hit the surface.

bodies.name: Deimos
bodies.note: The smaller and outer Martian moon, smooth with dust. From the surface of Mars it looks like a bright star.

bodies.name: Io
bodies.note: The most volcanically active body known. Tidal flexing from Jupiter and its orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede keep its interior molten.

bodies.name: Europa
bodies.note: A salt-water ocean with roughly twice the volume of Earth's lies under its ice shell. Europa Clipper, launched in October 2024, arrives in 2030.

bodies.name: Ganymede
bodies.note: The largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than Mercury, and the only moon with its own magnetic field. ESA's JUICE mission will orbit it in the 2030s.

bodies.name: Callisto
bodies.note: Its surface is the most heavily cratered known and has barely changed in four billion years. A deep ocean may lie beneath it.

bodies.name: Mimas
bodies.note: The crater Herschel is a third of its diameter. Its wobble suggests a young ocean under the ice, a surprise for so small and battered a moon.

bodies.name: Enceladus
bodies.note: Geysers at its south pole spray ocean water into space. Cassini flew through the plumes and found salts, silica, hydrogen and organic molecules.

bodies.name: Tethys
bodies.note: Almost pure water ice. The canyon Ithaca Chasma runs three quarters of the way around it.

bodies.name: Dione
bodies.note: Bright ice cliffs streak its trailing side. Gravity data hint at an ocean about 100 km down.

bodies.name: Rhea
bodies.note: Saturn's second-largest moon, an ancient cratered ball of ice and rock.

bodies.name: Titan
bodies.note: The only moon with a thick atmosphere and the only other world with stable liquid on its surface: lakes and rain of methane. NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft is due to launch toward it in 2028.

bodies.name: Iapetus
bodies.note: One hemisphere is as dark as coal and the other as bright as snow. A ridge up to 20 km high runs along its equator.

bodies.name: Miranda
bodies.note: A patchwork of mismatched terrain. Verona Rupes is a cliff about 20 km high, the tallest known.

bodies.name: Titania
bodies.note: The largest moon of Uranus, crossed by fault valleys hundreds of kilometres long.

bodies.name: Oberon
bodies.note: The outermost large moon of Uranus, old and heavily cratered.

bodies.name: Triton
bodies.note: It orbits backwards, which marks it as a captured Kuiper belt object. Voyager 2 saw nitrogen geysers rising 8 km from a surface at −235 °C.

bodies.name: Charon
bodies.note: Half Pluto's diameter. The two orbit a point in the space between them and keep the same faces toward each other.

bodies.name: Ceres
bodies.note: The largest object in the asteroid belt and the first asteroid found, in 1801. The bright spots in Occator crater are salts left by brine that reached the surface.

bodies.name: Pluto
bodies.note: New Horizons flew past on 14 July 2015 and found nitrogen glaciers, water-ice mountains and a blue haze. Its orbit is tilted 17° and crosses inside Neptune's.

bodies.name: Haumea
bodies.note: Spins once every 3.9 hours, which has stretched it into an ellipsoid. It has two moons and a ring.

bodies.name: Makemake
bodies.note: A bright, reddish Kuiper belt world covered in frozen methane, found in 2005.

bodies.name: Eris
bodies.note: Slightly smaller than Pluto but 27% more massive. Its discovery in 2005 forced the question of what counts as a planet.

bodies.name: Gonggong
bodies.note: A dwarf-planet candidate on a stretched 554-year orbit, slowly rotating and deep red.

bodies.name: Quaoar
bodies.note: Has rings far outside the Roche limit, where theory said they should have clumped into a moon.

bodies.name: Orcus
bodies.note: Shares Pluto's 2:3 resonance with Neptune but stays on the opposite side of its orbit, hence the nickname anti-Pluto.

bodies.name: Sedna
bodies.note: Never comes closer than 76 AU and swings out to about 940 AU over an orbit lasting some 11,400 years. It reaches perihelion around 2076, the only such chance for many thousands of years.

bodies.name: Vesta
bodies.note: The brightest asteroid and the source of a whole class of meteorites. NASA's Dawn orbited it in 2011–12 before moving on to Ceres.

bodies.name: 1P/Halley
bodies.note: The first comet recognised as periodic. It passed aphelion in December 2023, 35 AU out, and is now falling back toward its perihelion of 28 July 2061.

small.name: 16 Psyche
small.note: A metal-rich asteroid in the main belt that may be the exposed core of a failed planet. NASA's Psyche spacecraft, launched in October 2023, arrives in 2029.

small.name: 101955 Bennu
small.note: A 490-metre rubble pile. OSIRIS-REx brought 121.6 g of it to Earth in September 2023; the samples contain amino acids and all five nucleobases of DNA and RNA.

small.name: 162173 Ryugu
small.note: A carbon-rich near-Earth asteroid. Japan's Hayabusa2 fired a projectile into it, collected the debris and returned 5.4 g to Earth in December 2020.

small.name: Didymos and Dimorphos
small.note: On 26 September 2022 NASA's DART struck the small moon Dimorphos and shortened its orbit by 33 minutes, the first time humans changed the path of a celestial body. ESA's Hera is due to arrive in November 2026 to survey the result.

small.name: 99942 Apophis
small.note: On 13 April 2029 it will pass about 32,000 km above Earth's surface, inside the ring of geostationary satellites and visible to the naked eye. An impact has been ruled out for at least a century.

small.name: 486958 Arrokoth
small.note: The most distant object ever visited: New Horizons flew past on 1 January 2019. Two lobes that touched gently and stuck, preserved from the Solar System's first few million years.

small.name: 1I/ʻOumuamua
small.note: The first known visitor from another star system, seen in October 2017 already on its way out. Elongated or flat, with no visible coma, yet it accelerated slightly as if outgassing.

small.name: 2I/Borisov
small.note: The second interstellar object, found by an amateur astronomer in August 2019. Unlike ʻOumuamua it looked like an ordinary comet, unusually rich in carbon monoxide.

small.name: 3I/ATLAS
small.note: The third interstellar object, discovered on 1 July 2025 and the fastest of the three. It passed perihelion on 29 October 2025 and is leaving the Solar System.

craft.name: International Space Station
craft.note: Continuously crewed since 2 November 2000. It circles Earth about every 93 minutes at 7.66 km/s, some 420 km up, on an orbit tilted 51.6° to the equator. The ring drawn here is that orbit's height and tilt; where the station is on it is only shown on the Flight Deck when fresh tracking data is available.

craft.name: James Webb Space Telescope
craft.note: Launched on 25 December 2021. It orbits the Sun–Earth L2 point 1.5 million km from Earth, where a single sunshield can block the Sun, Earth and Moon at once. Its 6.5-metre mirror has seen galaxies from the universe's first 300 million years.

craft.name: Voyager 1
craft.note: Launched on 5 September 1977. It crossed into interstellar space on 25 August 2012. On 18 November 2026 at 10:16:07 UTC it becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: a command sent today arrives tomorrow.

craft.name: Voyager 2
craft.note: Launched on 20 August 1977, two weeks before its twin. The only spacecraft to have visited Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989). It crossed into interstellar space on 5 November 2018, and NASA expects it to reach one light-day in November 2035. Position here is approximate.

craft.name: New Horizons
craft.note: Launched on 19 January 2006. It flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015 and the Kuiper belt object Arrokoth on 1 January 2019, the most distant flyby ever made. Position here is approximate.

craft.name: Pioneer 10
craft.note: Launched on 3 March 1972, the first spacecraft through the asteroid belt and past Jupiter. Its last signal was received on 23 January 2003. It carries a plaque showing where it came from. Position here is approximate.

craft.name: Pioneer 11
craft.note: Launched on 6 April 1973 and the first spacecraft to fly past Saturn, in 1979. Contact ended in November 1995. Position here is approximate.
